# Why Rāvaṇa belongs in your address bar

Every address bar is a choice. When you type ​**Rāvaṇa**, you are not typing a novelty; you are restoring a name that the early DNS, built for English typewriters, could not carry. The plain ASCII form *ravana* is a leftover of ‌that constraint, not the name itself. This post is the long version of the restoration: where the name comes from, how the Devanagari tradition wrote it, how it is pronounced, what the myths ‌and the material record preserve, and why its Unicode form now lives as a working domain. The claim throughout is simple — the original spelling is not decoration. It is the name.

## ​At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Rāvaṇa
- **ASCII form:** ravana
- **Meaning:** "The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa"
- **Domain of influence:** Ten-Headed ​King, Lanka
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** Preserves vowel length
- **Original script:** रावण (Devanagari)
- **Live domain:** rāvaṇa.com

## Overview

**Rāvaṇa** (*ravana*) — Ten-Headed King, Lanka · The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, ​whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Ten-Headed King, Lanka". The name means "The ruler of Laṅkā ​and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa".

**Rāvaṇa** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is associated with ten-headed king, lanka.

PuniCodex restores the ​name as **Rāvaṇa** and serves its temple at [ravana.com](https://punicodex.com/ravana/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one ‌historically valid Unicode restoration exists. The plain ASCII form *ravana* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends ​as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **रावण**. Etymologically it means "The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of ​the Rāmāyaṇa".

Sanskrit Rāvaṇa, from the causative of rū 'to roar, to cry'; the ten-headed king of Lanka.

The ASCII form *ravana* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry ‌diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Rāvaṇa** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive ​feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **r** → **R** — Same, capitalized
- ‌**a** → **ā** — Macron: long vowel
- **v** → **v** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **ṇ** — N with dot: retroflex n
- **a** → **a** — Same

The canonical ​temple for this name is served at **ravana.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Sanskrit Rāvaṇa, from the causative of rū 'to roar, to cry'; the ten-headed king of Lanka.

The ‌root gloss is "the screamer."

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **रावण**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Rāvaṇa*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ​Sanskrit Rāvaṇa is written in Devanagari as रावण
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex ​articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ravana/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **R** — Initial character of the restored form Rāvaṇa.
- **āvaṇa** — Remainder of ​the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'RAVANA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

​Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — Rāvaṇa, the restored Unicode form of the name

Rāvaṇa preserves both features because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, ​or special characters.

## Mythology

The stories of **Rāvaṇa** circulate within the Sanskrit corpus, where the figure embodies ten-headed king, lanka.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Rāvaṇa is attested in the canonical Sanskrit sources as ‌a figure associated with ten-headed king, lanka.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa" ​and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Rāvaṇa** is the ten-headed king of Laṅkā and the antagonist of the *Rāmāyaṇa*. A devout śaiva and master of the Vedas, he abducts Sītā ‌and is ultimately defeated by Rāma, the avatāra of Viṣṇu. His character is morally complex: the epic praises his learning and power even as it condemns his lust and tyranny. His ten heads ​traditionally represent mastery of the four Vedas and six shastras, making him a scholar-king as well as a demon.

### Born of Sage and Demoness (Uttarakāṇḍa 9)

In the Rāmāyaṇa's seventh book the ‌villain's pedigree is nobler than his deeds: his father is Viśravas, a sage of flawless conduct, son of Pulastya, whom Brahmā generated from his own mind; his mother is Kaikasi, daughter of the ​daitya king Sumāli. From their union came four children — Rāvaṇa, the massive Kumbhakarṇa, the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, and the fierce Śūrpaṇakhā (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 9–11). The young Daśagrīva performed a tapas of terrifying ‌austerity — standing amid five fires, his arms raised, for a thousand years — until Brahmā, unable to refuse him, granted near-invulnerability: no god, gandharva, yakṣa, or demon might kill him. Men he ​omitted from the request, in contempt for their weakness (Uttarakāṇḍa 10). Later tellings deepen the bargain — nine times he offered his own head into the fire, and nine times it grew ‌back, until ten heads stood where one had been. The epic's point is exact: its monster is born of a sage's house, and his doom is written into his own wish.

### The Shaking ​of Kailāsa (Uttarakāṇḍa 16)

Striding forth to conquer the quarters, Rāvaṇa found the way to Śiva barred by the bull-bannered gatekeeper Nandin; mocked for his boast, he took hold of the mountain ​itself and began to wrench it from its roots, so that the peaks, forests, and every creature upon them cried out (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 16). Śiva pressed the peak down with the toe of ‌his foot and pinned the upstart's arms beneath it; the agony tore a roar from him so tremendous that the three worlds shook, and the pleased god named him on the spot: ‌Rāvaṇa, 'he who roars' — for older tradition the roar was the cry of the crushed, and Kālidāsa would later retell the whole confrontation in the Kumārasambhava (canto 7). Crushed but unrepentant, Rāvaṇa ‌sang — the Śivatāṇḍava stotra, the hymn still recited in Śaiva mornings — until the mountain lifted and Śiva, mollified, gave him the sword Candrahāsa. The myth defines him in a single ​tableau: strength enough to move a mountain, devotion enough to sing to the god who crushes him, and a roar that becomes his name.

### The Golden Deer (Araṇyakāṇḍa 40–52)

In the forest of ​Pañcavaṭī the king of Laṅkā played the long game of vengeance. His sister Śūrpaṇakhā came home mutilated by Lakṣmaṇa after her advances; his cousins Khara and Dūṣaṇa marched out of Janasthāna with ‌fourteen thousand troops and were annihilated. Then came the abduction itself: Mārīca, master of illusion, took the shape of a golden deer with silver spots, and Rāma, beguiled, chased it deep into the ​wood; the dying demon mimicked Rāma's voice crying for help, and Sītā — against her own knowledge of the rules of the forest — sent Lakṣmaṇa after him. With the hermitage empty, ​Rāvaṇa approached in the guise of a wandering ascetic and carried Sītā off through the sky in the Pushpaka chariot. The aged vulture Jaṭāyu, her only defender, struck until his wings were shorn ‌and fell dying; from his last words Rāma learned the abductor's name. Every element of that hour is answered in kind before the epic ends — the epic's economy of violence is ​exact, and the abduction buys the destruction of everything Rāvaṇa loves.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Rāvaṇa concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the ​name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Rāvaṇa carries the original marks of the Sanskrit tradition.
- **Source Script** — Preserved through scholarly transliteration and canonical sources.
- **Domain** — Ten-Headed King, Lanka
- **Etymology** ‌— The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa

- **Ten heads (daśānana)** — The multiplied mind; later tradition glosses the ten as ​the four Vedas and six śāstras — mastery worn as anatomy.
- **The Pushpaka vimāna** — His sky-going chariot, won from his brother Kubera — the vehicle of the abduction and, at the ‌epic's end, of Rāma's triumphal return.
- **The Śivatāṇḍava stotra** — The hymn he sang with crushed arms beneath Kailāsa — the one language, devotion, that he never lost.
- **Brahmā's boon** — Near-invulnerability to ​gods, gandharvas, and demons — and the fatal contempt that left men out of the list.
- **The golden city of Laṅkā** — The island fortress his brother Kubera ruled before him, built ​of gold by the divine architect Viśvakarman.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Rāvaṇa survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and ​each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Rāvaṇa is attested in the textual and iconographic record of the Sanskrit tradition.

## Realm & Domain

**Rāvaṇa** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, ​where it is associated with ten-headed king, lanka.

### Ten-Headed King

The central domain of Rāvaṇa in the sanskrit tradition.

### The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣ

The name signifies "The ruler ‌of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa".

### Unicode Restoration

The restoration Rāvaṇa recovers what plain ASCII ravana flattens.

### Original Attestation

Attested in ‌the sources as —.

### King of Laṅkā

Son of the sage Viśravas and the daitya princess Kaikasi; sovereign of the golden island fortress and its rākṣasa hosts (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa 9).

### Epic Attestation

Chief ​antagonist of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa — and, in the Jain Paümacariya, the noblest king of the story.

## Across Cultures

Rāvaṇa appears within the Sanskrit tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and ‌scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], and [[ganga|Gaṅgā]].

## Cultural Legacy

​Rāvaṇa continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Sanskrit tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes. Rāvaṇa remains ​a commanding figure in South Asian performance, from Rāmlīlā pageants to Tamil and Sinhala retellings that offer alternative perspectives.

## A Meditation

Rāvaṇa embodies ten-headed king, lanka in the Sanskrit imagination. The name's ‌restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.

## The Unicode Restoration

Rāvaṇa preserves vowel length. The ASCII fallback *ravana* ‌still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 1 mark of length (ā); 1 further ​adjustment (ṇ). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Character by Character

The journey from *ravana* to **Rāvaṇa**, one character at a time:

- **r** → **R** ‌— Same, capitalized
- **a** → **ā** — Macron: long vowel
- **v** → **v** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **ṇ** — N with dot: retroflex n
- **a** → **a** — ​Same

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **rāvaṇa.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--rvaa-qsa0806b.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name ​travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Rāvaṇa; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why ​a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Devanagari can now be typed into any browser on earth.

The [PuniCodex Type Tool](/type/) converts the ASCII form *ravana* into **Rāvaṇa** as you type, and the browser extension offers the same conversion inside any text field. ## Why This Restoration Matters

Restoring **Rāvaṇa** is part of a larger effort to make the web multilingual by default. ‌The PuniCodex project does not ask users to learn a new alphabet; it asks the infrastructure to respect the alphabets that already exist. Every section of this post — the script, the sound, ​the myths, the evidence — converges on the same point: the marks in Rāvaṇa are information, and information deserves an address of its own. A single Unicode domain is a small proof, ‌but it is a proof that scales: every name restored makes the next one easier, and every visit to rāvaṇa.com is a vote for the restored form.

## A Closer Look at the ‌Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Rāvaṇa**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *ravana* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a ​story. Of the 6 characters, 4 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word ​built from the same letters.

The **r** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **a** becomes **ā** — Macron: long vowel.

The **v** stays as it is — Same.

The **a** ​stays as it is — Same.

The **n** becomes **ṇ** — N with dot: retroflex n.

The **a** stays as it is — Same.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the ​minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it ‌was written.
